parsed.gloss: hazāroñ - thousands, ḳhvāhisheñ - desires, aisī - such, ki - that, har - every, ḳhvāhish pe - desire on, dam nikle - life was spent, bahut - many, nikle - came out, mire - my, armān - wishes/desires, lekin - but, phir - again, bhī - also, kam - few, nikle - came out
parsed.literal: Thousands of desires such that every desire took a life. Many came out from my wishes/desires, but again only a few came out.
parsed.poetic:
A thousand hopes I had, each one a soul to spare; many were born, but few could ever find their way to air.

(Transliterated: HazaroN khwaahishEsi kih har khwaahish pe dam nikle,
Bhut nikle mire armaan lekin phir bhi kam nikle.)
notes: The Urdu word 'armān' can mean both 'wishes/desires' and 'dreams', so I chose the former to maintain the balance of meanings. The phrase 'har khwaahish pe dam nikle' means that every desire took a life, as in it was pursued with all one's strength and energy. The poet is saying that his desires were numerous but only few came out successfully.

parsed.gloss: Neither was there anything nor was God; only God existed. If I had not been, what would I have been? (If I had never been born.)
parsed.literal: There was nothing but God; if I hadn't been, what would I be?
parsed.poetic:
I'd rather be than never be at all; there's no other choice for me to make.

 The only thing that I can say is God alone exists and nothing else remains.
notes: The poet plays on the ambiguity of 'kuchh' (something) and 'na hota' (not existing).

notes: The poet uses 'pankhi' (reed flute) to symbolize the fragility of the rose's petal, while also hinting at the delicate nature of her voice. The comparison between the reed flute and the rose emphasizes their shared vulnerability but also highlights the strength that lies beneath their seemingly fragile appearance.

parsed.gloss: All will pass, good and bad. The boat will cross just like that.
parsed.literal: Both good and bad will pass away. This boat will cross in this way.
parsed.poetic: Good and bad will come and go. The journey of life goes on.
notes: The Urdu phrase 'بری اور بھلی سب گزر جائے گی' means that both good and bad times will pass, suggesting the impermanence of life's experiences. The English translation maintains this meaning by using 'good and bad.' In the second line, the idiom 'یہ کشتی یوں ہی پار اتر جائے گی' refers to the journey of life as a boat crossing an obstacle. The English translation retains this imagery with 'The boat will cross just like that.' Both translations emphasize the continuity and unpredictability of life's experiences.
